name: Bakoko
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Kenmogne, Michel 2000. The lexical phonology of Bakoko (PhD thesis, 347pp; not found online)

new_statements.quote: Le ɓàkokò est une langue à tons, c'est-à-dire qu'en ɓàkokò, la hauteur mélodique est utilisée à des fins distinctives. Chaque voyelle du ɓàkokò porte un ton et signale ainsi un centre de syllabe. Cependant, il existe une nasale N̩ qui se comporte comme un noyau de syllabe, par conséquent elle porte aussi un ton, lequel ton est toujours bas en position initiale de mot. Il ressort de nos investigations les cinq tons suivants: [...] Les tons haut, bas, montant et descendant ont une valeur distinctive en ɓàkokò. Ils sont donc des tonèmes.
new_statements.translation: Bakoko is a tone language, that is, in Bakoko melodic pitch is used for distinctive purposes. Every Bakoko vowel bears a tone and thereby signals a syllable centre. However, there is a nasal N̩ that behaves as a syllable nucleus and consequently also bears a tone, which is always low in word-initial position. Our investigations yield the following five tones: [...] The high, low, rising and falling tones have distinctive value in Bakoko. They are therefore tonemes.
new_statements.citation: Edika, E. Solange Félicité. 1990. Esquisse phonologique du Bakoko (parler de Dibombari). Mémoire de Maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé, Faculté des Lettres et Sciences Humaines. 98 pp.
new_statements.locator: §I.1 'Inventaire des tons', p. 9 (PDF p. 13); tonemes p. 12 (PDF p. 16)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (102 PDF pages, Acrobat Capture scanned layer; pages 13, 16 and 17 rendered and read as images). The first block of the quote ("Le ɓàkokò est une langue à tons... Il ressort de nos investigations les cinq tons suivants:") is on thesis p. 9 = PDF p. 13, section I.1 'Inventaire des tons', word for word as quoted (the syllabic nasal is a hand-drawn N with a diacritic on the page; N̩ is a fair rendering). The second block ("Les tons haut, bas, montant et descendant ont une valeur distinctive en ɓàkokò. Ils sont donc des tonèmes.") is verbatim but sits at the top of thesis p. 13 = PDF p. 17 (end of I.2.4, before the 'Note explicative' and I.3 'Définition des tonèmes'), not p. 12/PDF…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. Bakoko is described as a lexical tone language (4 tonemes H, L, rising, falling; every syllable nucleus carries a tone; noun-class prefixes are always low). Stress/accent is not mentioned in any of the three accessible descriptions (Edika 1990, Njeck & Anderson 2010, Gehr 1914).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: mid tone occurs phonetically but is not a toneme; syllabic nasal is always low word-initially; prefixes always low (orthography guide, p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on the phonological word (citation forms from a wordlist; Dibombari dialect). Word-level stress is not treated; no phrase-level prosody described.
new_statements.identity_note: Edika 1990 describes the Dibombari dialect (the 'Yabyan-Yapeke' detached group in the Moungo, north-west of the main Bakoko area; no separate Glottolog dialect code known). Njeck & Anderson 2010 is a community-wide orthography (Centre Linguistique Bakoko), dialect not specified. Gehr 1914 describes the Sanaga-river Bakoko between Lobetal and Edéa (self-name 'Bakogo', Adie/Yakalak area). Glottolog lists Edika 1990 as a PhD thesis; the title page shows it is a Mémoire de Maîtrise. Wikipedia/ALCAM note that northern and southern Kogo are as distinct from each other as from Basaa.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent anywhere (no 'accent', 'intensité' etc. in the scanned text; TOC has no accent section). States Bakoko is a tone language: every vowel (and syllabic N) bears a tone; five surface tones, four tonemes H, L, rising, falling (mid not phonemic), pp. 9-12.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Kogo language' (accessed 2026-09-17), citing ALCAM 2012 dialect list and the SIL/CABTAL orthography guide.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; used only to locate the 2010 orthography guide URL and the dialect inventory.

sources.citation: Njeck, Mathaus M. (CABTAL) & Stephen C. Anderson (SIL). 2010. Bakoko Orthography Guide. Yaoundé: CABTAL (revised after the Bakoko orthography meeting of 24 Feb 2010). 16 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Section 3 Tone, p. 7: 'We have identified four surface tones in Bakoko: two level tones, high [á] and low [à], and 2 contour tones, rising [ǎ] and falling [â]'; functional load of tone low; all prefix tones always Low.

sources.citation: Gehr, Chr. 1914. Die Bakokosprache. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen 17, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 118-133 (prefatory note by D. Westermann).
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone; a missionary sketch of noun classes with example sentences, pronouns, verb forms and texts, no sound description at all (Westermann notes it is the first printed material on Bakoko). Sanaga-river Bakoko (Lobetal to Edéa), self-name Bakogo.

sources.citation: Skolaster (Scholaster), Hermann. 1914. Die musikalischen Töne in der Basa-Sprache. Anthropos 9: 740-759 [cited in the Routledge Bantu Languages bibliography as 'Basa Bakoko-Sprache'].
sources.note: About Basaa (A43a), not Bakoko: distinguishes Basaa 'dynamischer Akzent' from musical tone (pp. 743-745, e.g. 'Bei den durch die Zahl 2 gekennzeichneten Wörtern ruht der Starkton auf der zweiten Stammsilbe' for Basa nouns). Bakoko appears only in a Basa-Bakoko-Jaunde comparative word list (section 7, pp. 754 ff.) with no statement about Bakoko stress.
